Tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes are a significant factor in determining the effectiveness of cancer treatment and patient prognosis. However, accurately assessing their presence in tissue samples requires skilled pathologists, leading to a shortage of expert annotations and, subsequently, a lack of high-quality training data for deep learning models. To address this issue, we propose a federated learning approach for the multi-category classification of TILs. Our method enables a central server and multiple client nodes to collaborate on model development and data augmentation under data localization. We tested our federated learning framework on the TIL-8 classification task and achieved comparable results to models trained on fully centralized data, with performance even exceeding that of models trained on expert-pathologist-annotated data and 3D convolution-based models trained on whole-slide-image data. The source code of our approach is available on GitHub at https://github.com/zhaozhifeng1/FedTLIL.

Identifying unusual activities in video streams is a crucial aspect of several real-world applications, encompassing event detection in surveillance and action recognition in human-centric scenarios. Existing methods for detecting anomalies typically involve frame-level or segment-level processing, where frames or segments are initially generated according to a predetermined protocol and then analyzed for deviations from this protocol. This paper proposes a new framework called ReAD, which identifies unusual activities at a local level by dividing a continuous video stream into distinct segments. ReAD utilizes a neural network to detect anomalies within each segment and assesses their continuity using a self-information metric, ultimately determining the most unusual segments in the video stream. Comprehensive experiments were conducted on two public datasets to evaluate the performance of ReAD and demonstrate its superiority over current state-of-the-art methods. The source code for ReAD is available on GitHub at https://github.com/zhaozh/ReAD. The dataset used in this research can be accessed via https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1Q6Q6Q6G.

We introduce the Dynamically Weighted Inertial Forward-Backward (DWIFOB) algorithm to tackle monotonic inclusion problems in a broad context. This method seamlessly integrates a forward step with the Inertial Backward Forward (IBF) procedure and can be viewed as an evolution of the Forward-Backward (FB) algorithm with adaptively adjusted weights. non-stationary reward variations while adapting to changing evaluation criteria
in Markov decision processes. A key component of this model is a dynamic
bound on the optimal value function, which we use to develop two decision-making
algorithms. The first algorithm achieves the best possible results when the
non-stationary reward changes at a predictable rate, while the second algorithm

risk function and a technique for reducing the non-stationary reward variation
while maintaining a minimum level of exploration. Through theoretical analysis,

Our results show that flat bands give rise to a flat band resonance in the magnetoresistance at low temperatures, accompanied by a high-symmetry Dirac point. Furthermore, we found that electron interactions and flat bands synergistically contribute to an exceptionally high magnetoresistance in Pd$_3$Pb compared to its noble metal counterparts. Notably, this high magnetoresistance can be attributed to a flat band-induced correlation-enhanced mass adaptation effect. Additionally, we observed that a flat band resonance can also be observed in Pd$_3$Sb and Pd$_3$As, although it is obscured by other band structures in these materials. Our study provides a comprehensive understanding of the flat band properties in Pd$_3$Pd and related materials, shedding light on the origin of their exceptional magnetoresistance. Moreover, we propose that a flat band resonance can serve as a universal hallmark of flat band-induced magnetoresistance in multi-orbital flat band systems. Lastly, we suggest that flat band-induced magnetoresistance can be a versatile concept for enhancing magnetoresistance in various flat band systems.

This study aims to investigate how site-specificity affects resting-state connectivity measurements and provide guidelines for achieving precise connectivity predictions across various sites. We employed a systematic approach to evaluate the impact of site-specificity on connectivity research and used a large public dataset to demonstrate our findings. Our results show that connectivity measurements can vary significantly between sites and that generalizing these findings to new, unseen data from the same population is feasible. We also identified several factors contributing to site-specificity and developed recommendations for improving the accuracy of connectivity predictions and data sharing. These recommendations prioritize standardization, data quality control, and large sample sizes. Additionally, we introduced a novel metric for evaluating connectivity research and demonstrated its utility in assessing our findings. We hope that our study will facilitate data sharing and contribute to more precise connectivity predictions across various sites. Transition-based models have achieved remarkable success in NLP tasks, but their application in code-mixed language processing has been limited due to the difficulty of processing multiple languages at each transition step. To overcome this challenge, we propose a dynamic and relative positional representation model called PESTO, which uses a transition point encoder to capture relevant information from code-mixed sentences. The model consists of two key components: a relative representation module and a dynamic positioning module. The former generates positional information for all transition steps, while the latter determines the optimal positioning for the transition point. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of PESTO, with our model outperforming the baseline model by 1.5% and 3.5% in sentence splitting and part-of-speech tagging tasks for Swahili-English and Hindi-English code-mixed sentences, respectively. Furthermore, PESTO significantly reduces the number of parameters required by the baseline model, with a parameter reduction of 87% and 76% for Swahili-English and Hindi-English, respectively. The source code of PESTO is publicly available on GitHub.

Our calculations of the electronic structure and critical temperatures of hydrogen sulfide (H$_{3}$S) high-pressure superconductors reveal the significance of a van Hove singularity on its phase diagram. This singularity, which emerges under high pressure conditions, strongly influences the critical temperatures of H$_{3}$S superconductors, with their critical temperatures being more responsive to isotopic variations when the van Hove singularity is present. Our investigation revealed that different data source agents often produce distinct video search results, with the level of variability consistent across various query categories. Interestingly, we found that the disparity in search outcomes was more pronounced during periods of high search volume, suggesting that the underlying ranking models may be sensitive to source variability. Furthermore, we demonstrated that the disparity in search outcomes was not solely attributed to differences in search volume, but rather the diversity of available videos during high search periods. Our study provides a framework for assessing source variability bias in video search platforms and highlights the need for systematic evaluations that consider various data sources. We will publicly release our code and data to facilitate replication of our findings. Additionally, we will present our research at the 2022 IEEE International Conference on Multimedia and Expo. Graph Neural Networks excel in addressing various graph-based challenges, but their effectiveness heavily relies on accurate node labels, which can be difficult and costly to obtain. To overcome this limitation, we propose a novel pseudo-labeling technique that leverages a pre-trained GNN to generate high-quality node labels for the entire graph, rather than just supervised nodes. To prevent noisy pseudo-labels from contaminating training, we employ a self-supervised loss function that evaluates pseudo-label consistency across neighboring nodes. Experimental results on Cora, Citeseer, and Pubmed datasets demonstrate our method to be more effective than current GNN semi-supervised training techniques. Additionally, our code is available for public access at https://github.com/zhaozh/PSL.

In laparoscopic surgery, smoke formation during tissue burning can distort the surgeon's vision, making precise tumor-removal and organ-identification challenging. To mitigate this, we investigated whether pre-processing the images to reduce smoke interference could improve detection accuracy. Focusing on a specific task, we analyzed the impact of smoke on identifying the cholecystoscope in fundus detection. Our study revealed that smoke impeded performance but pre-processing the images did not necessarily enhance it. Smoke's effect was found to be task-dependent and, interestingly, pre-processing might not always be beneficial. This led us to conclude that image enhancement should be applied selectively, based on the specific task at hand. Additionally, we proposed a novel pre-processing method, smoke-removal filter, which was found to be effective in certain situations. This research contributes to the understanding of smoke's influence on medical image analysis and could guide the development of more robust algorithms. In interior point methods, an iterative solver is employed to solve a linear equation. We propose introducing an interior termination criterion for generalized minimum residual methods and conjugate gradient methods. This new criterion will enable the solver to stop iterating when an optimal solution's center remains within the interior of a feasible region. Our experimental results demonstrate that this criterion results in significantly fewer iterations of the solver when utilized in interior point methods for linear programming and quadratic programming. This new criterion exhibits a cactus effect, reducing the number of iterations. We also present an interior version of the Anderson acceleration technique that can be applied to any Krylov solver. This accelerated method can be paired with the interior termination criterion for enhanced performance. Our numerical evaluations confirm that this acceleration results in a substantial reduction in iterations. This acceleration and the interior termination criterion synergistically boost the efficiency of the solver when utilized in interior point methods. The interaction between two processes can be formalized as a dual specification, which is typically achieved by linking two finite-state automata in a specific configuration. This monitoring approach enables real-time analysis of the interaction, allowing for the identification of discrepancies between the observed interaction and the specified dual process. In this context, we introduce a method for handling disagreements between the two processes, which may occur due to various issues like ambiguous specifications or process limitations. This work presents a novel technique for dual process monitoring that incorporates dispute management, which is founded on automata theory and provides a method for identifying discrepancies between the observed interaction and the specified dual process. Additionally, we provide a method for resolving disputes by determining the minimum adjustments required for both processes to align with the specified dual process. This method is shown to be effective through experimental validation using real-world scenarios. Specifically, we demonstrate its application in monitoring the interaction between a self-driving car and a backseat passenger. This work is part of a broader research that explores the use of automata theory in monitoring dual process specifications. Further details can be found in a separate paper. We investigate the scaling characteristics of exceptional elements within random matrices and matrix-free frameworks. Outlying elements in generalized eigenvalue problems exhibit a distinct scaling regime in both the strong and weak matrix scenarios, leading to the identification of a universal scaling limit. This regime is further linked to a critical parameter in the matrix polynomial eigenvalue problem, where we demonstrate the existence of a scaling limit and determine the associated universal spectrum. Numerical support for our findings is also provided through stochastic outlierness metrics and eigenvalue density estimates. Moreover, our analysis yields a novel universality class for exceptional generalized eigenvalues and a new critical dynamic for outlying elements in matrix pairs. This research significantly expands the scope of outlying behavior in low-probability events, shedding light on the global behavior of exceptional elements in linear algebra and related statistical frameworks. Assembling genomes from short, overlapping DNA sequences is a computationally complex task, particularly challenging with long DNA sequences. A new parallel algorithm has been developed to create contiguous sequences from sequences stored in a global array, enabling the assembly process to be accelerated. This algorithm uses a partitioning scheme to assign sequences to processors' local memory, minimizing memory usage by selecting non-overlapping sequences. Our method efficiently creates contiguous sequences with a minimal memory overhead, outperforming existing assembly tools in speed and memory usage. A variant of this algorithm has been applied to genome assembly, resulting in significant speed improvements of up to 3.6 times and reduced memory usage of over 80%. The implementation is publicly available in the SpArk library.

The moments were calculated by analyzing the hyperfine structure in the 283.7 nm transition of GeI, a molecule composed of a Ge atom and a chlorine anion. In lattice field theory, Standard Weingarten functions play a crucial role in regulating ultraviolet divergences in physical computations. This tutorial aims to provide an accessible foundation for lattice field theory practitioners to understand the principles of flow-based weingarten functions, which offer a dynamic approach to volume dependence. We will delve into the underlying theory, starting from the basic concepts of semigroups and operator flows, before exploring the properties of Standard Weingarten functions and their implementation in lattice field theory. This report is based on a series of lectures delivered at the 2019 INT Workshop on Lattice Field Theory. Due to space constraints, further details can be found in the cited reference and additional online resources.

This research focuses on enhancing the Structured Text Identification task by leveraging a new type of favoring relation. The STI task necessitates identifying specific text segments within documents to maintain structural integrity. To accomplish this, we introduce the Regular Expression Favoring relation, allowing models to infer segment structures from annotated examples, similar to how regular expressions capture targeted patterns in text. This novel relation complements existing favoring relations, and our experiments demonstrate that models incorporating this new relation exhibit improved performance on the TAC Structured Text task. Furthermore, we created a substantial dataset containing regular expressions by re-examining prior TAC Structured Text challenges and annotated data from the CoQA dataset. This dataset, along with our findings, is accessible through a public repository. Our models' optimized codes are also available for reproduction. This study was initially published in the EACL 2021 conference.

High-energy proton-nucleus collisions offer a unique laboratory to study how top quarks and other heavy particles behave in environments with varying inter-quark potential and color fields. A key challenge in analyzing these processes lies in accurately identifying the top quark's production and distinguishing it from background noise. In this study, we simulate top quark generation in proton-nucleus collisions using the NLO QCD framework and develop a novel, efficient method to distinguish top quark signals from background events, particularly in the case of collinear proton-lead collisions at the LHCb energy scale. By applying this method, we estimate the signal-to-noise ratio for detecting top quark generation in collinear proton-lead collisions and isolated proton-proton collisions. This study paves the way for further research on top quark detection in proton-nucleus collisions at fixed-target laboratories and in other non-collinear proton-nucleus setups. Additionally, we discuss potential future experiments at the LHCb and the Fixed Target on LHC projects that could significantly enhance top quark detection sensitivity. In these experiments, the reduced color fields in the nucleon and nuclear targets could facilitate top quark generation detection via the D-zero meson signature. This study opens up new possibilities for exploring top quark generation in a diverse range of proton-nucleus collision environments. Developing a text-to-SQL parser that can handle various domains is a challenging task, particularly because each domain has its unique set of SQL operations and semantic concepts. To address this issue, we propose a new framework that allows for zero-shot parsing across different domains. This framework consists of two main components: a cross-domain language model and a supportive task model. The language model is trained to learn domain-invariant text-to-SQL meaning from a database containing multiple domains, while the supportive task model is designed to provide essential semantic information that facilitates parsing in unfamiliar domains. Through experiments on the SPIDER dataset, our framework has demonstrated enhanced parsing capabilities in domains without explicit annotations. Notably, our framework has achieved a 6.9% absolute improvement in execution accuracy compared to the baseline model. The code for this research is available on a GitHub repository.

The LoTAR catalogue contains 13,645 galaxies with redshifts between 0.05 and 0.25, spanning a dynamic range of 10^4 in luminosity. Our analysis reveals a power-law energy spectrum with an index of approximately -1.5, consistent with semi-analytical models and previous observations. Furthermore, we have identified distinct biasing patterns for different galaxy populations, which are influenced by their stellar mass. We have also found that the LoTSS galaxies exhibit a negative density-temperature relation, consistent with the thermal feedback hypothesis. The observed biasing patterns are in good agreement with the predictions of semi-analytical models, suggesting that these models accurately represent the underlying dark matter distribution. However, some discrepancies remain, particularly at very large scales, where the LoTSS galaxies show a more gentle slope than the models. These surveys will extend the redshift range to 0.6 and increase the dynamic range by two orders of magnitude, enabling a more comprehensive understanding of the relationships between galaxies, their environments, and their spectral properties. In a scenario of preferential exchange, consumers make purchasing decisions by prioritizing goods based on their relative prices and availability. When human judgment is involved in determining whether a consumer's purchasing choices align with a proposed price structure, the concept of structural equilibrium comes into play. This paper explores the relationship between this concept and the idea of views, which represents a theoretical framework for evaluating the plausibility of a consumer's purchasing decisions. We establish that, in a scenario with a single good of interest, a consumer's behavior will be considered structurally consistent if their responses to price changes are predictable and coherent, leading to a satisfactory outcome under equilibrium conditions. Furthermore, we show that a high level of views is both a necessary and sufficient condition for a satisfactory outcome under equilibrium conditions, and that views can be seen as an alternative measure of a consumer's behavior that is comparable to the concept of limited assurance. We also introduce a new metric, which we term "view assurance," to quantify the level of confidence in a consumer's behavior and its relationship to the concept of limited assurance. View assurance is found to be a necessary condition for a satisfactory outcome under equilibrium conditions, and we propose a method for obtaining a lower bound on view assurance as an indicator of a consumer's behavior and price structure alignment. This research contributes to the development of a framework that can provide assurance that a consumer's behavior and price structure alignment are consistent, which has practical applications in areas such as pricing and revenue management. To create engaging stories, it's essential to effectively use time-series data and convey a clear narrative structure. Current storytelling models, however, focus on specific application areas and don't easily adapt to other domains. To address this limitation, we present TCube, a novel neural story generation model that can effectively use time-series data without being tied to a particular domain. TCube achieves this by using a flexible template system that allows stories to be structured around the development of key values over time. We evaluate TCube's performance on two diverse datasets, showcasing its ability to outperform existing story generation models while also providing a deeper understanding of its generated stories. TCube's implementation is available at https://github.com/chenyifeng/TCube.

Medical professionals rely heavily on medical records, which are typically written in a free-text format, to gain valuable insights into patients' conditions. Extracting significant events from these records and organizing them in a standardized manner is crucial for medical research and clinical decision-making. However, the current approach to extracting these events is mostly confined to a specific hospital setting and would require substantial revisions to work elsewhere. In this paper, we introduce a new task known as domain generalization for sign event extraction, which enables a model to extract meaningful events from records without being limited to a particular domain. We also establish a large-scale dataset consisting of medical records and create a benchmark for this new challenge by providing multiple domain-specific training sets with a shared representation. Our experimental results demonstrate that a model pre-trained on a task called sign BERT is capable of performing well on this new generalization task. The dataset and benchmark are now available for public use at https://github.com/linzhi2006/Domain-Generalization-SE.

The rising complexity of modern electronic systems is driving up real estate costs, leading to increased power consumption and heat production. Compact Footprint Integrated Systems (CFIS) are becoming essential to addressing these issues by minimizing component size and spacing. However, implementing CFIS requires precise timing relationships between signals, which can be challenging to achieve with smaller components. This study introduces an Automated Operator Assessment tool to facilitate CFIS design by identifying the optimal CFIS structure from a given set of logic functions and signal paths. This innovative approach distinguishes itself from existing time-sequential logic design methods by incorporating a unique time-series analysis technique to streamline CFIS design. Furthermore, the tool can evaluate and compare the effectiveness of different CFIS configurations, serving as a valuable design aid. Experimental results demonstrate the tool's efficiency in reducing CFIS size and signal complexity, thereby reducing design complexity and latency. Additionally, the tool's versatility allows it to be applied to various CFIS architectures such as Reconfigurable Pipelined Integrated Logic (RPIL) and Time-Sequential Integrated Logic (TSIL). The tool's source code is available on GitHub for public access. This research contributes to the field of integrated logic by providing a practical design solution and a theoretical foundation for CFIS assessment and optimization. The study also presents an in-depth analysis of CFIS design metrics and presents two CFIS benchmark circuits for public evaluation. The Automated Operator Assessment tool has been successfully validated through extensive simulations using the ISCAS'85 and the LGSynth91 benchmark circuits. The programmable phase disk in modern TEMs allows for adjusting the wavefront of the illuminating electron beam, enabling various applications like optimizing resolution or creating off-axis holography. This research investigates its potential to rectify aberrations affecting electron microscopy images. By simulating the phase disk as a plane in three-dimensional space and calculating its effect on the wavefront, we determined its capabilities to counter spherical and coma aberrations through simulations. The results indicate that the phase disk can effectively mitigate spherical aberration, but its ability to correct coma aberration is heavily dependent on the sample's position. Due to the phase disk's circular shape, it cannot be positioned at the back focal plane of the objective lens, which is necessary for correcting coma, leading to the conclusion that it cannot entirely replace an aberration corrector. Nonetheless, the phase disk remains a valuable feature for optimizing resolution and supporting holography-based imaging techniques. Additionally, the code used in this research is publicly accessible on GitHub.

We introduce MaskedSpeech, a context-sensitive speech synthesis model that leverages a masking approach to generate natural-sounding speech. By selectively masking phonemes during decoding, MaskedSpeech inserts contextually relevant replacement phonemes into the speech waveform. Our model outperforms previous research in non-autonomous speech synthesis, achieving improvements of 8.6 and 12.9% in phoneme accuracy on the VCTK and LibriTTS datasets, respectively. Furthermore, we demonstrate that MaskedSpeech's phoneme insertions are directly audible in the speech waveform. To facilitate reproducibility, we provide the full code and pre-trained models at the https://github.com/alexyu2019/MaskedSpeech repository.

Artificial intelligence and machine learning classifiers are vulnerable to manipulation by adversaries who launch targeted attacks. A specific type of assault, which we term a person-in-the-middle (PIM) attack, involves an attacker intercepting data from a victim and altering it before sending the modified data back to the victim's classifier. This process exploits weaknesses in the training of deep learning models, particularly the assumption that input data will be continuous and varied, and can easily scale to affect multiple victims and classifiers. In this research, we explore the effectiveness of generative models in facilitating PIM attacks and assess their performance using metrics such as data similarity and attack success rates. Our experiments demonstrate that generative models can successfully alter inputs to achieve higher classification outcomes in the victim's system. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of training dataset size on the efficacy of these models and find that a larger training dataset leads to improved performance in some cases but also increases data reuse, which negatively affects the models' ability to generate unique and varied inputs. Our analysis also reveals that the complexity of the classifier affects the ease of launch and success rates of PIM attacks, with simpler classifiers being more susceptible to these attacks. Finally, we discuss potential countermeasures against PIM attacks and suggest future research directions. The code for this research is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/ahmed-omar/generative-pim-attacks.

Climate change deniers on social media frequently disseminate baseless online conspiracy theories, which often gain traction by targeting well-known celebrities and celebrities-in-the-making. Our investigation, centered on English-language Twitter posts, reveals that conspiracy theories centered on climate change typically concentrate on alleged plot shifts rather than outright denial. We have identified 134 distinct conspiracy theory variants, which are predicting the abrupt demise of climate change awareness or action by social media influencers. The rapid dissemination of these conspiracy theories is further accelerated through retweeting, resulting in higher engagement rates compared to conventional posts. Our analysis also uncovers the role of low-credibility information sources and bot-like Twitter accounts in disseminating conspiracy theories. Furthermore, we have identified 72% of these conspiracy theories prior to the verification of related climate-related crises on Twitter. Our findings suggest that the spread of conspiracy theories through social media poses a significant threat to climate change communication. To mitigate this, we propose targeted interventions focusing on the core message of conspiracy theories and involving influential social media personalities. Our study's methods and data are available for public use.

The proposed model treats image partitioning as a process of minimizing a multi-area partitioning energy function, where each area's characteristics are defined by a set of images or parameters. Our results show that the proposed method can effectively create meaningful partitions, even with noisy input images. We also applied our model to the creation of color-grade images, where we defined the characteristics of each area by their color properties. Our numerical experiments demonstrate the creation of visually appealing color gradients. Additionally, we applied our model to the image inpainting task, where we defined the characteristics of each area by regions of interest, and our results show successful feature recovery even in noisy areas. Our code is publicly available on GitHub.

This research introduces a multi-task neural network called the ImprovedReader network, designed to enhance low-quality handwritten document images. The network consists of an adversarial component that minimizes distortion during image improvement. We evaluated the network's effectiveness using a diverse dataset of 1,500 scanned handwritten documents, which includes various forms of degradation and 11,500 high-quality text images. The results demonstrate that the ImprovedReader significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in text readability, while also effectively removing noise and reducing distortion. Furthermore, the network's adversarial training enables it to perform better in our dataset. The source code and dataset are available on GitHub for reproducibility purposes.

A theoretical design for an optical metastructure is presented that can control and direct line defects in a two-dimensional array of holes in an electrically conducting material. This metastructure features a dual, symmetric unit cell with a small hole in each corner, allowing for the propagation of line defects along two distinct directions. By adjusting the hole dimensions in one direction, the line defect propagation in the other direction can be selectively switched on or off. This concept has been successfully tested and optimized in both theoretical designs and numerical simulations, showing promise for controlling line defects in optical and terahertz applications. Furthermore, a method for adjusting the line defect propagation is proposed, allowing for potential integration into an optical directional coupler. This design has the potential to be fabricated using advanced techniques such as E-beam lithography. This study provides a comprehensive analysis of the line defect properties, including their phase, phase velocity, and attenuation. In this study, we examined the characteristics of quarkonium disintegration in a 5-dimensional QCD environment with non-zero momentum anisotropy and finite baryonic chemical potential. We utilized the quasi-particle Debye mass to determine how quarkonium states behave in this complex system. Our findings indicate that, for a given quarkonium state, its binding energy changes sign at a specific value of the Debye mass, m_D. We also discovered that quarkonium disintegration is more pronounced when the system is highly anisotropic and that increasing baryonic chemical potential enhances quarkonium disintegration. Our research further reveals that, in the absence of momentum anisotropy, quarkonium states exhibit temperature-dependent ground state mass characteristics. However, when momentum anisotropy is introduced, this effect is replaced by a complex pattern in the quarkonium binding energy. Our study also demonstrates that, in the absence of baryonic chemical potential, the quasi-particle Debye mass is solely dependent on the temperature, but that introducing baryonic chemical potential adds an additional, baryonic mass component. Our findings are consistent with previous studies on the characteristics of quarkonium disintegration in a 5-dimensional QCD environment with non-zero momentum anisotropy and finite baryonic chemical potential. Deep learning-based classifiers for jet identification have achieved high accuracy, but their inner workings remain difficult to understand. To improve transparency, we developed a new method that uses expert variables to represent and clarify the decision-making process of deep learning classifiers in jet identification. This method can be applied to other problems as well. 

We began by selecting key features from jet events that experts agree on, then used these to reframe the decision-making process of the classifier. We discovered that the original classifier was highly effective but relied on features it wasn't trained on. To further clarify its choices, we analyzed the inner workings of its layers, highlighting the relevant features used in each stage. 

This new method has several benefits: it helps us understand complex processes, identifies potential weaknesses, and enables us to pinpoint features that may be sensitive to data bias. Additionally, it allows us to use existing expert knowledge to guide and clarify the decision-making process of deep learning classifiers. 

We applied this method to a real-world problem, specifically to a deep learning classifier that identifies $b$-jets in $Z$-$\gamma$ decays at the Large Hadron Collider. We used expert variables to represent the classifier's decision and analyzed its inner workings, revealing that it relies on features that may be sensitive to data bias. 

To further investigate, we analyzed the spread of relevance throughout the layers of the classifier. We found that the relevance of features spreads unevenly, with some features remaining highly relevant while others become less important. This led us to consider alternative methods that could give more equal attention to all features. 

This research demonstrates that the new method can clarify the decision-making process of complex classifiers and provide insights into their inner workings. We hope this will contribute to more transparent and understandable AI models.

This paper investigates the effect of framework exploration in unverified assertions within SMT solvers. Unverified assertions in interactive proof assistants serve as a framework for guiding search within SMT solvers. By categorizing model variables, unverified assertions direct the SMT solver to explore relevant cases, enhancing its efficiency. However, the current method of asserting variables does not account for the framework in which they reside. As a result, the SMT solver may waste time examining unrelated variables or ignore pivotal ones within the framework. To address this limitation, we introduce two new assertions: "exploring-in" and "exploring-out," which enable the SMT solver to focus on variables within the selected framework. Our experiments demonstrate that incorporating these assertions significantly boosts the SMT solver's performance in generating interactive proofs. Furthermore, we present a strategy for automatically generating "exploring-in" assertions, thus streamlining the process of creating interactive proofs. Lastly, we showcase the incorporation of these assertions in a verified framework for generating interactive proofs within the Coq proof assistant. This verified framework, along with the SMT solver and Coq plugins, are available for public use.

This framework enables us to identify two essential loss function properties that influence convergence and generalization. We then conduct experiments to demonstrate the loss function property's impact on training deep neural networks and showcase their value in optimizing model performance. Furthermore, we develop a method to numerically evaluate loss function properties during training, allowing for the development of adaptive loss functions that adjust their parameters based on training progress. Our findings and the theoretical framework offer insights into loss function design, contributing to the development of more effective deep learning models. The code for this research is publicly available at https://github.com/alexkamath/loss-assessment.

This research investigates the evolution of data complexity in modern Western music by analyzing the lyrics of top 10 hit songs from the US Billboard Hot 100 chart spanning the years 1964 to 2019. We employed the Shannon entropy measure to quantify complexity and found a significant increase over the study period. However, examining the entropy of individual song titles revealed a different pattern, with no clear evolution. We also discovered that the most popular songs in each decade tend to have higher complexity than lesser hits, indicating that success in the music charts is linked to complexity. Furthermore, our analysis suggests that the complexity of song lyrics is influenced by the words used in song titles. This paper explores the relationship between computability and the concept of playfulness, aiming to illuminate its foundations. By drawing parallels between the harmony of music and well-founded recursion in computability, we establish a framework for playfulness. This leads to a concept of 'harmony sets' that can be used to model intuitionistic mathematics and a related propositional logic. We also demonstrate that this playfulness corresponds to the effective topos of a certain constructive set theory. Furthermore, we show that the playfulness is consistent by constructing an intuitionistic semantics for the related type theory. Additionally, we discuss the relationship between playfulness and other foundational approaches. Finally, we provide a simple example of a harmony set that is not a Scott domain. Reward learning in autonomous systems poses a significant challenge due to the vast number of possible reward functions.  To address this issue, we propose an approach that leverages human feedback to assign groups of trajectories with similar behaviors.  By allowing humans to label these trajectory clusters rather than individual actions, we increase efficiency while maintaining the ability to learn complex behaviors.  We evaluate our method in simulated 3D environments and find it to be a more time-effective approach for learning trajectories compared to traditional reward learning.  Additionally, our approach can be used to support other ranking learning methods and we demonstrate this by successfully training a controller for a 3D navigation task.  We also provide a public implementation of our method, including source code, trajectory clustering tools, and evaluation metrics.  This can be accessed via https://github.com/robotics-aba/cluster_ranking. We introduce a parameterized version of upward planarity that considers the number of rotations as the parameter. Two parameterized classes of upward drawing schemes are defined: fractional linear upward drawing and linear upward drawing. The Fractional Linear Upward Drawing class can be solved in polynomial time by applying the parameterized version of the Constrained Fractional Linear Layout problem. Additionally, a parameterized algorithm for constructing linear upward drawings is presented, taking into account the number of rotations required. This algorithm is based on a novel technique that relates linear upward drawings to planar straight-line drawings with certain constraints. This research introduces a new learning paradigm, Indecision Forests, designed to acquire complex, argument-based reasoning in difficult cases. Typically, machine learning models struggle with such reasoning, often producing overconfident mistakes. Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is a complex neurological condition characterized by excessive hyperactivity, inattention, and impulsivity. Although the standard diagnostic approach involves a comprehensive evaluation of a child's behavior by a psychologist or psychiatrist, accurate and efficient diagnosis remains a significant challenge. Recent advancements in Deep Learning (DL) techniques have shown promise in developing algorithms capable of differentiating ADHD patients from controls using resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI) data. This study investigates whether a DL-based approach can accurately diagnose ADHD by focusing on specific brain regions that exhibit distinct patterns of connectivity. By analyzing rs-fMRI data from the Human Connectome Project (HCP) dataset, we identified 20 crucial regions that were used to train and test various DL models. Our results indicate that a combination of spatial attention and gradient-boosting-based learning outperforms other methods in classifying ADHD patients, achieving a high accuracy of 85.3%. Notably, this accuracy surpasses previous DL-based approaches that utilized the entire rs-fMRI dataset without spatial filtering. Furthermore, our study highlights the importance of distinct connectivity patterns in the default mode network (DMN) in ADHD, specifically the reduced connectivity between the anterior cingulate cortex and posterior cingulate cortex. Additionally, we demonstrate that our model can accurately identify ADHD patients using reduced spatial information, achieving a high accuracy of 83.4% when utilizing approximately 40% of the original spatial dimensions. This study provides valuable insights into the critical brain regions involved in ADHD and shows that DL-based approaches can effectively diagnose the condition using rs-fMRI data. Our findings have the potential to inform clinicians and researchers about the underlying neurobiological mechanisms of ADHD. Moreover, our model can be employed for developing diagnostic tools that leverage rs-fMRI data to enhance ADHD diagnosis and treatment. The code and data used in this study are publicly available at https://github.com/ahmedebaid/ADHD-diagnosis-with-rs-fMRI.

Topological insulators are known for being immune to certain types of distortions while allowing wave propagation along their edges. A new topological feature has been discovered in momentum space, characterized by nodal surfaces that separate topologically distinct regions. This novel property has been observed in various structures, including those without a lattice, and can be found in both optical systems and GRACE gravitational waves. This review focuses on the theoretical aspects of nodal surfaces as topological features in momentum space and recent experimental implementations in optical systems and others. It also discusses the distinct characteristics of nodal surfaces compared to other topological features. Additionally, the potential applications of nodal surfaces in optical systems are explored. Furthermore, the relationship between nodal surfaces and topological features in real and energy spaces is examined. Finally, the challenges and future directions for research in this area are identified.

the spatial variation. This paper presents new analytical approximations for the 
velocity of these pacemaker-generated waves, which are compared with existing 
methods and found to yield accurate results with minimal computational expense. 
Furthermore, we investigate the dependence of wave velocity on the system's 
parameters and the applicability of our approach to both coupled neural and chemical 
reaction systems. To validate our method, we also conduct numerical simulations in 
two-dimensional spaces, demonstrating excellent agreement between our analytical 
estimates and the simulated wave velocities. This approach can be applied to a 
variety of oscillatory media in both biological and chemical contexts. Additionally, 
we discuss the potential extension of our analytical framework to describe wave 
propagation in more complex systems with multiple pacemaker sources. This study 
provides a new tool for the wave dynamics community to utilize the pacemaker model, 
enabling the rapid estimation of wave velocities based on system parameters. 
Finally, we explore the connection between our analytical results and the concept of 
local activation and inhibition, which is a widely employed model in neuroscience. 
This connection holds particularly true for neural systems with a linear spatial 
dependence. However, it also extends to nonlinear systems, as evidenced by our 
two-dimensional numerical simulations. This relationship between pacemaker models and 
local activation/inhibition models may facilitate the application of our analytical 
estimates to a broader range of systems. This approach can be adapted for use in 
biochemical reaction systems with a significant temporal variation, as illustrated by

Temporal association analysis is a key method for identifying disease progression and disease interaction patterns using electronic health records. However, the International Classification of Diseases (ICD) codes used to represent diseases and events lack clear semantic meaning, making it difficult for clinicians to define relevant association rules beforehand. This study proposes a novel approach that combines semi-supervised learning and conditional random fields to enable rule specification with patient data and post-hoc validation with clinical expertise. Our technique was tested on a large dataset of patients with chronic kidney disease and diabetes, demonstrating significant improvements in accuracy and F1-score when applied to temporal association analysis. The study's findings highlight the potential for this method to facilitate the discovery of disease progression and interaction patterns without extensive pre-defined rules. The implemented system and experimental data are available online.

Shadows play a crucial role in rendering realistic images and have numerous applications in computer vision. However, accurately calculating shadows in complex 3D environments remains a challenging task. In this study, we present an innovative, diffused shadow model that is highly efficient and differentiable, enabling easy integration into various computer vision methods. Our model's unique formulation allows for the calculation of shadows using simplified equations, eliminating the need for iterative ray-tracing methods. Moreover, it can be optimized using backpropagation, making it suitable for end-to-end training. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our model through quantitative comparisons in both rendering and computer vision domains. The code is openly available on GitHub at https://github.com/zhengyu-lyu/diffused-shadows.

Historically, two popular algorithms have been used to randomly generate a uniform spanning tree from a connected graph. The Aldous-Broder algorithm and Wilson's algorithm are notable examples. Traditionally, it was believed that these algorithms operated independently, but we demonstrate that Wilson's algorithm produces a temporary equivalence to a modified Aldous-Broder algorithm, resulting from a two-phase framework for generating uniform spanning trees. This temporary equivalence occurs when the graph is constructed in an online manner. Furthermore, we show that any algorithm used to generate a uniform spanning tree can be converted into an equivalent form within our proposed framework. This conversion does not affect the tree's generation time and maintains linear-time efficiency for the resulting spanning tree. Additionally, we provide a verified Coq proof for the temporary equivalence. This finding offers insights into the underlying properties of spanning trees and potentially expands the applicability of the two-phase framework to other combinatorial objects. As a practical application, we present a dual implementation of the two-phase framework in C, showcasing its utility. This work may serve as a foundation for further research into the underlying properties of spanning trees. The music transcription task has received significant attention in recent years, with a particular focus on breaking down the transcription process into more manageable sub-tasks such as score rendering and text-to-audio synthesis. Achieving these sub-tasks requires the development of multi-format datasets that can bridge the gaps between sheet music, lyrical text, and audio. This paper introduces the MusicTM-Dataset, a comprehensive collection of 10,000 songs that enables the creation of unified representations for these three formats. The dataset is designed to facilitate the training of a single model capable of performing multiple tasks, and we provide experimental results demonstrating the effectiveness of this approach. The MusicTM-Dataset is currently accessible at https://github.com/valhelin/MusicTM-Dataset.

This study introduces an innovative approach to analyzing large datasets of linked information by leveraging word embeddings similar to those used in natural language processing. By applying this method to Ontodia and Wikidata, we enable data examination with interactive visual tools, facilitating experts to gain insights into conceptual models and related knowledge graphs without the need for specialized word embedding training. Our solution offers a general framework for visual analysis, as demonstrated by two use cases showcasing its effectiveness. The first application involves exploring the distribution of word embeddings among Ontodia's domain concepts, revealing hidden patterns and correlations. The second case enables users to identify and visualize key terms associated with biomedical articles, uncovering their semantic connections and context-dependent meanings. To support these use cases, we have developed a publicly accessible demo and documented the underlying methodology in a research paper. Additionally, we have contributed two new extensions to the Wikidata Query Service to streamline the preprocessing of word embeddings for large datasets. These extensions include WordEmbeddings and ConceptLinkage, facilitating the linking of word embeddings to Wikidata concepts and enhancing the visual analysis experience. Our solutions are now available online for public use.

In a complex visual environment, effective object recognition relies on distinguishing between visually similar objects. This study investigates how recurrent neural networks (RNNs) utilize visual cues to identify individual objects in a group of four familiar objects (cube, sphere, cylinder, and triangle). By analyzing the RNN's internal state and its relationship to the objects, we demonstrate that the RNN exploits unique characteristics among these objects to classify them correctly. These characteristics are organized in a hierarchical manner, with one aspect (shape) used more frequently than others (size and orientation). The RNN's internal state is found to be highly distinctive for each object, with its classification performance significantly impaired when the RNN's internal state is artificially mixed. This study provides the first evidence that RNNs rely on category-orthogonal object characteristics for identification. Additionally, we show that the RNN's internal state is learned during training and is resilient to noise in the input. Finally, we propose that the RNN's internal representation may be interpreted as a mental template for each object. This study offers a new perspective on how artificial neural networks understand and process visual information. Its findings and methods can be applied to investigate the information processing in animal brains and to develop more efficient algorithms for object recognition. A key assumption in machine learning is that data reflects an underlying reality with consistent meanings. However, this premise is challenged when dealing with sequential tasks that involve manipulating information to achieve desired outcomes, a scenario better explained by a signaling game model. To address the issue of emergent semantic shifts, we propose a neuro-symbolic approach that integrates causal inference and signaling dynamics within a shared framework. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through a case study of semantic exchanges in a product description task. Our approach not only handles semantic changes but also outperforms existing state-of-the-art models in semantic parsing, while providing insights into its decision-making processes. The proposed framework is now open-source at https://github.com/DeepSysteam/SEEG.

We introduce a novel approach to session-based suggestion, combining two-phase 
recommender systems that utilize rank representations of candidates. In the first 
phase, suggestions are generated based on general preferences, while the second 
phase refines these suggestions by incorporating users' session-specific 
interactions. A candidate representation method is then applied to update the 
suggestion pool. This two-phase framework generalizes existing session-based 
recommender systems and is evaluated across four datasets, demonstrating 
improvements in suggestion quality through refined candidate representations. 

We further propose a new candidate representation method, MRRP, which outperforms 
alternative representations, including matrix factorization and graph 
convolutional neural networks. The framework and representation method are 
demonstrated to enhance the quality of suggestions in various domains.

This research demonstrates the feasibility of neural speech synthesis without a language model by utilizing acoustic-based transliterations that are derived directly from speech. These transliterations are converted into standard text using a set of pre-defined units and their interconnections, which are in turn used to train a sequence-to-sequence synthesis model. Evaluations on the TIMIT dataset reveal that this approach yields speech samples of comparable quality to those generated from transliterations obtained through automatic speech recognition. Furthermore, the synthesized speech is shown to be more similar to its acoustic counterpart than speech synthesized from rarer, speaker-independent phonemes. Ultimately, this method offers a means of neural speech synthesis in data-sparse and resource-constrained environments. A new statistical method for determining required sample sizes in clinical trials is presented, designed to accommodate multiple subpopulations. This approach utilizes Bayesian principles to balance individual subgroup power needs and overall trial efficiency. Two metrics are proposed to quantify information exchange between subgroups: one measures similarity in treatment effects and the other assesses shared knowledge through posterior distribution overlap. Formulas for calculating desired sample sizes are developed and illustrated with examples. Results indicate that this approach can substantially reduce the total number of patients required compared to methods that disregard information between subgroups. A basket trial in oncology is used to demonstrate the method's efficacy. Two subpopulations were examined, and the approach successfully determined how to combine their data to achieve desired precision levels. This approach is made available through an R package named "BayesSSBE". This package includes functions for estimating required sample sizes, evaluating information exchange, and generating trial simulations. Deep generative models face significant challenges when working with unlabeled modalities, making it difficult to define a suitable objective function. Our proposed Cyclic Division Generative Adversarial Network (CDGAN) overcomes this limitation by partitioning data into two categories and training them separately, allowing for unsupervised cross-modality synthesis. CDGAN uses a discriminator to divide real data into authentic and fake parts, while two separate generators create authentic parts from fake data and entire data from authentic parts, respectively. Notably, CDGAN can be applied to various unsupervised cross-modality synthesis tasks, including image, domain, and cross-task synthesis. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of CDGAN in multiple scenarios. The source code is available at https://github.com/zhaozheng1994/Cyclic-Division-GAN.

Predicting the next action in a sequence of interactions is a complex task that has been approached through various future action prediction models. These models aim to identify the most probable actions that will occur within a specified time frame following the current state. Existing methods, such as RNN and CNN-based models, have been less effective in action prediction compared to models utilizing a different architecture, the Gru4l model. This model, incorporating Gru units and attention mechanisms, outperformed others by leveraging a feature mapping technique. Building upon this success, we introduce the Feature Mapping LSTM (FM-LSTM) architecture, integrating an LSTM unit with a feature mapping layer. FM-LSTM enhances the Gru4l model by utilizing a different type of recurrent unit, leading to improved performance. Our experiments demonstrate that FM-LSTM surpasses the Gru4l model, as well as other state-of-the-art methods, in action prediction. The code and models used in this study are available on GitHub at https://github.com/DeepAction/FMLSTM. FM-LSTM has been applied to the dataset from the Joint Action Recognition and Future Action Prediction Challenge (JRFAPC) at ACML 2019. This dataset comprises human action images, along with future action predictions. Our approach successfully identified the top three places in the track 1 competition of this challenge. Additionally, we have evaluated FM-LSTM on other action prediction datasets, such as NTU-RGBD and JHMDB-21. The results show that FM-LSTM outperforms other state-of-the-art models on these datasets. Our study highlights the effectiveness of FM-LSTM in future action prediction, along with its potential to be used in other sequence forecasting tasks. FM-LSTM can be used in a wide range of applications, including autonomous driving and robotic motion planning. Its ability to forecast future actions enables it to be utilized in scenarios where the system needs to predict what will happen next in a sequence of interactions. This characteristic makes FM-LSTM a valuable tool for various system designers. Our study also showcases the versatility of FM-LSTM by applying it to different action prediction datasets and demonstrating its ability to be used in a variety of settings. FM-LSTM can be used to improve the performance of other state-of-the-art models, as shown in our experiments. Our study highlights the importance of using feature mapping in action prediction, as well as the effectiveness of LSTM units in this task. FM-LSTM has been successfully applied to both action and future action prediction, along with other sequence forecasting tasks.

To efficiently label data under a tight budget, we propose a multi-instructor distillation framework that effectively trains a strong model with the help of multiple human annotators. PILE is a straightforward, fast, and reliable method that outperforms existing approaches, achieving substantial gains in our experiments. To improve this shortcoming, we introduced two higher-order Raviart-Thomas elements, which provided more accurate results. Specifically, the new elements had second-order accuracy in homogeneous domains and first-order accuracy in heterogeneous domains. These new elements were also stable in diverse scenarios, including both theoretical and practical contexts. Moreover, we demonstrated that they could be constructed with the same level of computational complexity as their lower-order counterparts. To achieve this, we employed novel approaches to prove that certain discrete operators are continuous. These results expand the existing theory of the vector conveyance equation and provide a reliable numerical tool for solving the equation. Furthermore, we verified the efficacy of the new elements through numerical experiments. To facilitate the use of these new elements, we provided a comprehensive implementation in the FEniCS project. Long video activity recognition has become increasingly prominent in recent years, with the rise of low-cost, high-quality cameras. The key challenge lies in designing models that can effectively span short to long time frames. This study presents a novel hierarchical model, Focus Network, which comprises a local detail module and a global main module. The local module enhances feature resolution through multi-scale local attention, while the global main module leverages global attention to focus on crucial details. Our model achieves top-notch performance on the LongVid-30 dataset and Kimera dataset, outperforming previous benchmarks. The study also showcases the model's ability to recognize activities across extended periods. The model's code and LongVid-30 dataset can be accessed via a dedicated repository.

We have developed a design for an on-chip single-photon source consisting of a ridge waveguide coupled to two adjacent III-V semiconductor quantum emitters in close proximity. This leads to exceptional mode confinement and minimal loss rates of approximately 0.05 dB per unit length at the quantum emitters' resonant frequencies. Our design also features a 95% effective coupling of the quantum emitters' resonant frequencies to the WGM resonator. This exceptional performance positions our design as a leading approach for on-chip single-photon source applications. We propose a logical framework that supports continuous reasoning by defining a category where morphisms are represented as confidence functions. This framework extends standard proof-theoretic semantics, allowing for infinitary sequents and multisorted signatures. We demonstrate that the established operational and proof-theoretic semantics in NPFLTL can be translated into this logical framework. Furthermore, we show that the category's unit and composition operations have direct connections to the framework's multisorted and infinitary nature. Finally, we present a simple example to illustrate the use of this logical framework. We examine the nonadiabatic extension of Born effective charges in crystalline solids, calculating these charges for the first time in a general way. In metals lacking a bandgap, we show that the charges can be defined and computed using a linear response approach, and that they reduce to standard Born charges in adiabatic cases. Our explicit computations for hcp and fcc structured metals reveal that the Drude masses derived from their transverse sound modes align closely with our calculated Born charges. Additionally, we applied these charges in the analysis of piezoelectric polarization in bcc magnesium. Our results also imply that the absence of bandgaps doesn't preclude the existence of spontaneous polarization or dielectric polarization in metals. Lastly, we discuss the practical applications of these charges in the study of phonon-electron interactions. Our code for these calculations is publicly accessible on the GitHub platform.

The system's sensitivity to these fluctuations leads to chaotic behavior, characterized by unpredictable fluctuations. The time lag is found to amplify this chaotic behavior by a large factor, often exceeding thousands or millions. The resulting chaotic patterns persist even after the system reaches a stable equilibrium state. The underlying mechanism involves the system's inability to eliminate periodic and random fluctuations due to its complex delay structure. We establish a semantics for the probabilistic lambda calculus using probabilistic transition systems, drawing on concepts from measure theory and probability theory. By leveraging a lifting technique, we demonstrate the equivalence of two established semantics: one grounded in Kleisli composition and the other in streaming semantics. Furthermore, we show the sufficiency of a weak form of this semantics, defining a valid probabilistic lambda calculus and proving its soundness and completeness. The developed methods are then applied to investigate the relationship between probabilistic lambda calculus and probabilistic Kleene algebras. The underlying technical framework provides a general approach for dealing with probabilistic models in category theory. The proofs are detailed in an accompanying appendix.

In the design process, conversations between designers and engineers produce valuable documentation that can be leveraged to create detailed product designs via specifications. However, these conversations often contain ambiguous or irrelevant information, hindering the effective creation of specifications. To address this, we propose a natural language processing-driven approach to filter out unessential discussion topics and ensure designers agree on key product features. We demonstrate the long-term reliability of our proposed method by testing its conclusion-stable nature, even when faced with different initial conversation selections. This is achieved by developing a set of mathematical concepts and an associated framework, called Conclusion Stability Framework, which serves as a universal evaluation standard for design conversation mining methods. We also provide a mathematical proof showing our approach satisfies this rigorous standard. To date, this work constitutes the first instance of a formally proven conclusion stability result for design conversation mining methods. We showcase the efficacy of our method by successfully creating detailed specifications for two complex products using a reduced, filtered version of the design conversations. We compare our approach with a competing method, highlighting its superiority in generating more accurate specifications with less discussion topics. This research opens up new avenues for formally evaluating design conversation mining methods and ensures their reliable adoption in the design process. Additionally, it presents an innovative application of mathematical concepts from the learning theory to the design domain. This research introduces a transfer learning-based approach to classify and identify damage to roads from various countries. The method is based on a pre-trained Road Transformer and utilizes a cross-entropy loss function with a mix of challenging images to enhance model performance and adaptability. The results show significant improvements, with the lowest error rate of 12.04% for road damage classification and 16.94% for sub-damage type classification, surpassing the baseline performance by 10.04% and 6.15% respectively. Moreover, the model demonstrates excellent potential for road damage classification in other countries, with error rates 50-60% lower than the baseline. The model's outstanding performance and adaptability make it an ideal solution for real-world road damage identification and classification. The source code and dataset are available on GitHub for public use.

Deep generative models have shown great promise in creating realistic synthetic data, but their application in imitation learning remains limited. Imitation learning aims to teach an agent how to perform a specific task by providing it with examples of the desired behavior. When the environment in which the demonstrations were collected differs from the one the agent needs to perform the task, the problem becomes even more challenging due to differences in observation and action spaces. We present a new method called Cross-Domain Mimicry Network (CDMNet) that can learn to perform a task as shown in observations from pre-recorded demonstrations in a different context. The network learns to bridge the domain gap between what it observes and what it needs to perform by using an adversarial loss, resulting in improved performance compared to previous approaches. The effectiveness of our method is demonstrated through successful imitation of diverse tasks, including reaching, door opening, and button pressing, collected under different camera perspectives. We also show that our method outperforms previous approaches in complex scenarios with moving obstacles. The synthetic trajectories generated by our method serve as a short-cut for agents to learn complex paths that would be difficult to achieve through reinforcement learning. This research explores the complex relationships between audio, visual, and thermal signals for creating a robust, feature-rich dataset that can be used for person authentication. Our study demonstrates the effectiveness of combining audio-visual-thermal modalities to improve identification accuracy. We present a novel authentication framework that integrates multimodal correlations and outperforms single-modality systems by a significant margin. Our dataset and authentication method are available online for further exploration. 

\textbf{Keywords:} Multimodal system, audio-visual-thernal, person authentication, identification, deep learning, correlation, modalities fusion. 

\textbf{Thesis:} Multimodal systems are more resistant to variability and uncertainty in identification processes. 

\textbf{Method:} Our research employs a multimodal dataset and an authentication framework that fuses audio, visual, and thermal signals to improve identification accuracy. 

\textbf{Dataset:} Our study utilizes a diverse, publicly available dataset containing face, skin, and audio recordings of 150 individuals under various conditions. 

\textbf{Framework:} Our authentication method involves three main components: face, skin, and audio feature extraction, followed by a fusion process that integrates these features and correlates the modalities for robust identification. 

\textbf{Results:} Our results show that the proposed framework outperforms single-modality systems and demonstrate high accuracy in challenging scenarios with varying illumination, skin texture, and background noise. 

\textbf{Conclusion:} Our research successfully integrates audio, visual, and thermal signals to improve identification accuracy and provides a robust framework for person authentication. 

\textbf{Future Work:} Our study can be extended to incorporate more complex scenarios, such as head pose variations and occlusions. 

\textbf{Code and Dataset:} Our research code and dataset are available online for further exploration.

Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of our model over existing solutions on the Fashion-Intra dataset. Additionally, we provide a detailed analysis of our model's performance and offer a code implementation for public use.

The extreme ultraviolet (XUV) field of a high-order laser pulse can be manipulated to produce attosecond XUV pulses via coherent manipulation. However, the natural electromagnetic field of the laser is often too strong for generating isolated attosecond pulses in high-order harmonic generation. We present a new scheme that uses a weak pump field to achieve robust, isolated attosecond pulses in harmonic generation. This weak field, either elliptical or linear, triggers a quantum electrodynamics process that creates a transient cavity and enhances high-harmonic generation. We observed that the pump field's polarization influences the generated attosecond pulses, resulting in two possible scenarios: either the pulses are produced with a consistent phase or their phases are modulated in a sinusoidal pattern. We have analytically and numerically demonstrated this concept, and the resulting attosecond pulses exhibit high peak powers, long lifetimes, and a high recurrence rate. These pulses offer promising possibilities for applications in nonlinear optics, metrology, and physics. Additionally, the generated pulses can be exploited to study the dynamics of single electrons and fast electron dynamics in atoms and molecules. Due to the long lifetime of these pulses, they can be used to investigate various phenomena, such as the interference of single electrons, without being affected by the pulse's decay. We envision that our approach will contribute to the development of a new class of coherent light sources with unprecedented properties. These light sources will enable us to study the behavior of matter on an extremely short timescale and potentially open up new avenues for controlling and measuring ultrafast processes. Moreover, our approach can be extended to other types of high-field pulses, such as those produced by chirped pulse amplification lasers, to generate even shorter attosecond pulses. We anticipate that our research will pave the way for a deeper understanding of quantum dynamics and the development of innovative methods for controlling and measuring ultrafast processes. Furthermore, our approach can be used to create new types of attosecond pulses with variable phase, which can be employed in various applications, such as coherent imaging, electron injection, and quantum computing. We have demonstrated that our approach offers a high degree of flexibility in generating different pulse types and can be easily adapted to various experimental setups. We have shown that our scheme can be used to generate pulses with variable phase and can be modified to produce pulses with a consistent phase by exploiting elliptical pump fields. We have also found that our approach can be used to generate pulses with a sinusoidal phase modulation and have identified the conditions necessary to produce these pulses

Physics-informed neural networks have shown remarkable potential in solving partial differential equations, but their widespread use is hindered by the choice of network architecture and node distribution. In this work, we introduce a new approach to creating training points for physics-informed neural networks based on the principles of residual reduction. The proposed technique adaptively places training nodes in areas where the residual error is highest, leading to improved convergence rates and more accurate solutions with reduced training data. Our experiments demonstrate that this method surpasses existing node creation techniques in a range of scenarios. Additionally, we provide a theoretical justification for the proposed technique and its connection to regularization methods. Furthermore, we showcase its effectiveness in solving challenging partial differential equations in dynamics and dynamics with discontinuities. The implementation details are available on our website.

This work presents a comprehensive simulation and analysis of a ferroelectric FET (FeFET) that incorporates multiple domains in the ferroelectric material, highlighting the role of domain walls that exhibit negative capacitance properties. We examine how these domain walls, triggered by a gate voltage, expand to encompass the entire channel area, resulting in a significant increase in the channel polarization. This polarization behavior gives rise to an exceptionally steep subthreshold slope, accompanied by substantial on/off ratio improvements. To validate our simulation findings, we develop a simplified electrostatic model that effectively captures the multi-domain FeFET's behavior and the negative capacitance phenomenon. Additionally, we investigate the impact of various domain wall-related properties, such as domain expansion speed and domain wall pinning, on the device performance. Finally, we explore the device's reliability through the simulation of random domain expansion and assess its endurance under repeated write operations. Our study provides a thorough understanding of the multi-domain FeFET's operation and paves the way for the design of these devices. Moreover, we envision that our work will contribute to the development of innovative CMOS-compatible ferroelectric technologies.

Various graph convolution functions have been proposed for point cloud processing, yet there's a lack of a comprehensive evaluation of their effectiveness. This has led to inconsistent results and difficulty in selecting an optimal GCN model for a given task. To address this issue, we provide a thorough analysis and comparison of different graph convolution functions, offering a benchmark for future research and a guide for model selection. Our study also introduces an open-source platform for reproducible research in GCNs. Furthermore, we present a novel graph convolution function, GCN-DNN, which achieves superior performance in point cloud semantic segmentation. Deep neural networks are susceptible to 'backdoors,' which can be triggered remotely and cause network outputs to be manipulated. Most existing backdoor techniques rely on modified network weights during training and require hidden 'trigger channels.' In this research, a new type of backdoor, called Semantic Hostless Trojan Assault (SHTA), is proposed. SHTA involves altering network outputs during training and triggering them remotely without requiring specific 'trigger channels.' Our experiments demonstrate that current defense methods are ineffective against SHTA and a proposed framework, called CleanTrigger, can successfully eliminate backdoors. CleanTrigger achieves high accuracy in classifying clean samples and trigger statuses, with results showing improved robustness against various defense methods. Code for this research can be found at https://github.com/zhaozhhy/SHTA.
