Achieving dependable learning in the presence of failures necessitates using multiple, redundant models. To handle node and communication failures during dependable learning, we propose regional all-reduce, a set of algorithms that utilize the infrastructure's topology to perform reliable data aggregation. Our analysis shows that using regional queries significantly boosts the performance of dependable learning by reducing communication overhead. We found that regional all-reduce can be up to 5 times more efficient than standard all-reduce and can handle a large number of failures without substantial performance degradation. Moreover, our regional all-reduce algorithms scale better than existing solutions, reducing dependable learning's communication complexity by a factor of at least 4 compared to previous approaches. We also found that regional all-reduce can be applied to other distributed neural network training algorithms, further improving their performance. Our experimental results show that regional all-reduce outperforms existing solutions by 1.5 to 4 times in real-world datasets and can handle a large number of failures without performance loss. By integrating regional all-reduce into training, we achieved 4% to 10% accuracy improvements in CIFAR10 and ImageNet. Our code is available at https://github.com/chenyong85/Regional-AllReduce.

This research investigates how heat affects the structure and mechanical properties of simulated Martian and lunar soil. The study utilized two types of simulant materials, one from Mars and one from the Moon, both of which were compacted using a 450 MPa press. The samples were then heated to 1000, 1100, 1200, 1300, 1400, 1500, and 1600 K in an electric furnace. X-ray computed tomography was used to examine the internal structure of the samples, while uniaxial compressive strength was used to evaluate their mechanical properties. The results showed that the internal structure of the samples became more porous as the temperature increased, with the largest pores forming at 1600 K. The mechanical properties of the samples also declined as the temperature rose, with the compressive strength of the Martian simulant decreasing by 83% and that of the lunar simulant decreasing by 76%. These findings provide essential information for future lunar and Martian bases, where materials will be subjected to similar heat treatments. The data can be used to predict the effects of high temperatures on soil and plan accordingly. Additionally, the research offers insights into the geological history of Mars and the Moon, with implications for future construction projects. Based on the findings, it is recommended that building foundations be constructed at least 1 meter below the surface to avoid temperature-related damage. The research also suggests that the mechanical properties of the samples can be improved by using a phase-change material to regulate temperature fluctuations. The study's recommendations are expected to contribute positively to the development of future lunar and Martian settlements. Type Ia supernovae (SNe Ia) play a crucial role in cosmology due to their bright peak luminosity, allowing them to be observed at vast distances. However, their spectra exhibit complex time-evolving characteristics that have yet to be fully utilized. We introduce a novel stochastic autoencoder model to capture the time sequences of SNe Ia spectra. The autoencoder's encoder transforms the high-dimensional spectral data into a lower-dimensional latent space, while its decoder generates stochastic samples from this reduced space to reconstruct the original spectral time series. We applied and validated our model on a simulated dataset of 1000 SNe Ia spectra with 51 data points and wavelength ranges of 3000-7000 $\AA$. The model's performance was evaluated using the mean absolute percentage error and the normalized wide image fit score, demonstrating that our autoencoder surpasses a comparable vanilla autoencoder. Furthermore, we successfully applied the model to a real SNe Ia dataset of 122 spectra. The latent space of our autoencoder exhibits promising characteristics, enabling the identification of distinct supernovae groups and allowing for the prediction of their phases using supervised regression techniques. The model's potential benefits and limitations are discussed, along with suggestions for future research. The code and data used in this study are publicly available at https://github.com/zhengyuzh/SNIA_SAE.

In recent years, deep learning has become a preferred approach for multimodal
machine learning tasks. Despite numerous studies on multimodal neural networks,
many of them focus on linearly combining different modalities, which can result
in significant information loss. To address this issue, we propose a new
framework called the Generalized K-fan Multimodal Neural Network, which allows
for non-linear combination of modalities through the K-fan layer. This new
network features a shared representation for improved learning of common
features and efficient fusion of non-linear modalities. We also introduce
optimization techniques tailored to the K-fan layer to enhance training. Our
experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed network on two
datasets, achieving superior performance compared to state-of-the-art models.

Developing correct multithreaded programs is challenging due to the complex interplay of concurrency, shared variables, and potential deadlocks. Current concurrency libraries in programming languages like C and C++ can lead to errors in safe multithreaded programs by providing data structures that are not thread-safe. Our model checker, McMini, identifies potential program crashes by modeling concurrency-related issues. McMini supports a range of synchronization primitives and data structures, allowing for the verification of multithreaded programs that use these primitives. Our tool is designed to be configurable and adaptable to new data structures and primitives, making it possible to extend the McMini model to cover additional concurrency scenarios. In our evaluation, we successfully applied McMini to various concurrency bugs in order to generate human-readable error reports and provide fixes. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of McMini in identifying potential issues and guiding the improvement of multithreaded programs. McMini is available at https://github.com/CSUNYC/ McMini.

The rapid dissemination of information on WhatsApp and similar messaging platforms plays a significant role in spreading misinformation, which has significant real-world implications in politics and public health. In an effort to counter this issue, WhatsApp introduced a feature limiting the number of groups to which a single message can be forwarded. Our proposed framework combines local device updates with server-side parameter adjustments using an entropy-based regularization method for effective parameter regulation. This approach enables seamless communication and prevents overfitting by stabilizing parameter fluctuations. This study examines how regional news outlets in the U.S. covered the COVID pandemic and how their coverage varied based on the severity of the outbreak in their areas, as well as the demographics of their audiences. Analyzing articles from 2019 to 2021, we found that regional news outlets initially underreported the pandemic, but as cases surged, they increased coverage. When deaths rose, coverage surged even more. Our findings also suggest that local news outlets serving areas with higher COVID severity and populations with higher vaccination rates reported more pandemic stories. Moreover, we discovered that older, more educated, and conservative audience demographics were more likely to encounter pandemic-related coverage. Our research provides insights into the relationship between local news coverage, COVID severity, demographics, and vaccination rates. It also underscores the importance of accurate pandemic reporting and the varying levels of COVID-related information received by different demographic groups. As federated learning gains popularity, protecting the integrity and confidentiality of model updates and data has become a major concern. This research addresses both confidentiality and integrity risks by developing an enhanced framework, FLVoogd. This framework builds on existing solutions, incorporating techniques such as virtualization, homomorphic encryption, and secure multiparty computation to safeguard data confidentiality. To mitigate insider threats, FLVoogd incorporates techniques like trapdoor generation, verification, and rectification to ensure the integrity of model updates, and employs a robust protocol for handling malicious clients. We evaluated our framework using EMNIST and MNIST datasets, and demonstrated its resilience against various types of attacks, including single and multi-client attacks and data poisoning attacks. Furthermore, our framework was shown to provide an acceptable level of performance loss while maintaining the accuracy of the trained model. The framework is available in open source at https://github.com/AmrYoussef82/FLVoogd.

Closing the gap between simulated and real-world settings in autonomous navigation presents a significant challenge. The framework's core component is a gradient-based sensor interface module that synchronizes the simulated model with real-world sensor data. The module's effectiveness is demonstrated through a series of experiments, including navigation tasks, which show that the developed approach outperforms state-of-the-art model adaptation methods. The source code for this project is publicly available on GitHub.

Inspired by the human brain, spiking neural networks have been developed for AI applications, particularly for pattern recognition tasks. However, the learning process in these networks often relies on backpropagation, which may not be biologically plausible. We introduce a new learning algorithm for spiking neural networks that combines temporal backpropagation through the dynamic memory in the brain with a gradient-free, regularization-based method inspired by genetic principles. This algorithm enables the networks to learn patterns in a biologically feasible way and outperforms traditional deep neural networks on various pattern learning tasks. Furthermore, our results show that the trained spiking neural networks can function efficiently even with significant numbers of neurons and time steps, simulating the dense connectivity and dynamic synaptic interactions observed in the brain. This work introduces a method to evaluate the accuracy of generalized polynomial chaos expansions (GPC) outside of the initial approximation stage. This method is demonstrated by verifying a GPC representation of the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations in a finite domain with initial condition error and external data perturbation factors. The associated error analysis relies on the smoothness properties of the solutions to these equations, which are known to be $W^{2,\infty}$. The results of this study confirm the effectiveness of our proposed method in assessing the accuracy of the GPC representations. The corresponding numerical implementation is detailed, along with a comprehensive set of test cases that demonstrate the method's utility. Deep model training faces significant time and resource constraints when working with large datasets and complex models. Model pruning offers a solution by reducing the model's size before retraining, but current methods often distort the model architecture, leading to suboptimal performance. We introduce ClickTrain, a new framework combining fine-grained pruning and architecture preservation to achieve better results. ClickTrain consists of an efficient training method and a novel, precise pruning technique that minimize error and preserve the model's original structure. Notably, ClickTrain allows for the retraining of pruned models with a fraction of the time required by the original model, while still achieving superior results. Recent breakthroughs by LIGO and VIRGO allow for the analysis of gravitational waves produced by mergers of neutron stars and black holes. Their detection opens doors to studying extreme physics and celestial events, as well as neutron stars that were previously undetectable. This paper presents a deep learning approach that uses gravitational wave data to identify and categorize events involving neutron star-black hole collisions. Our model uses a combination of convolutional and recurrent neural networks to process waveforms from various angles and assign them as binary neutron star-black hole events. We trained and tested our model on a dataset containing 246 neutron star-black hole signals, achieving a 99.7% accuracy in classification and 97.5% accuracy in binary neutron star-black hole classification. This model can significantly reduce the computational time required for future parameter estimation studies involving neutron star-black hole events, allowing for a more efficient analysis of these events with the upcoming third generation of gravitational wave detectors. Additionally, the study showcases a system-level integration of handwritten recognition and LaTeX generation, which significantly enhances its overall performance. The MathQA-Dataset and corresponding model implementations are publicly accessible.

Actor-critic reinforcement learning is a popular approach due to its efficiency in policy optimization. However, policy representation and its gradient estimation pose significant challenges, particularly when using a stochastic policy. To address these issues, actor-critic methods often employ variance-reducing techniques or maximize-expectation policy gradients. This paper introduces a novel actor-critic framework that integrates Hamiltonian Monte Carlo to efficiently sample transitions and optimize policy gradients. By leveraging the Hamiltonian Monte Carlo method, our approach can learn from a family of policies that are more flexible than traditional maximum-expectation policies. We evaluate our method on various reinforcement learning tasks and demonstrate its effectiveness in reducing variance and improving policy gradient estimates. As a result, our approach achieves better performance compared to state-of-the-art actor-critic methods. A publicly available implementation of our method can be accessed via GitHub.

micron wavelength, obtained from New Horizons' measurements, to identify the 
composition and mixing of its surface materials. By comparing the observed 
reflectance spectra with synthetic models of various icy and organic mixtures,

of these findings for our understanding of Nereid's geological history and 
differentiation processes. However, the analysis of Nereid's surface features 
revealed that some of the observed spectral patterns cannot be satisfactorily 
explained by the analyzed mixtures, highlighting the necessity for further 
spectral analysis and additional observations in the 1.5-2.5 micron wavelength,

for the analysis of Nereid's tholins and ammonia-cryogenite components, 
unfortunately not accessible in the New Horizons' spectral range. This study

In the context of dynamic treatment regimes, our proposed approach builds upon a conservative learning method that prioritizes minimizing potential losses in future treatment options. We demonstrate that this enhanced conservative learning strategy not only maintains the same level of safety as existing pessimistic methods but also achieves a significantly faster convergence rate compared to previous research. We also introduce a new Bayesian framework for conservative learning and show that it can be implemented with an affordable computational cost. We validate the efficacy of our approach through simulations and a real-world application in the field of geriatrics. Our findings indicate that this method not only provides more accurate predictions but also enhances existing pessimistic learning methods in dynamic treatment regimes. Additionally, we found that it outperforms other machine learning techniques in the specific use case studied. The R code used in this research is available on GitHub for public access.

Our findings suggest that certain methods excel in both scenarios, while others perform better in specific contexts. A comprehensive evaluation framework is proposed, incorporating metrics such as the number of clusters, cluster stability, and a novel score function based on clustering performance and feature selection. This research introduces an innovative salient item detection approach, capable of identifying key objects in both RGB and RGB-D images. A novel network architecture, comprising of a Fusion Module, RGB Module, and MD Module, is proposed to achieve this task. The Fusion Module effectively fuses RGB and depth information to generate high-quality salient masks. The RGB Module leverages a dual-stream decoder architecture to produce accurate salient masks from RGB input. The MD Module is designed to enhance depth-based salient mask prediction and improve overall results. Extensive experiments demonstrate the superiority of the proposed framework over existing methods. Furthermore, the framework's general applicability is shown through successful cross-dataset and domain adaptation experiments. The framework's source code and datasets will be publicly available.

This study presents the UM-IU@LING system's approach to identifying offensive content in tweets at SemEval 2019. We initially explored the utility of BERT and BERT-POV, two advanced language models, in offensiveness classification. However, our experiments revealed that they did not significantly outperform a basic SVM model. Consequently, we chose to submit an SVM-based solution to the task. In the pre-processing stage, we removed tweets containing URLs and applied the TF-IDF vector space model to convert the data into numerical form. The resulting data was then divided into training and testing sets. Various features were extracted and used to train different SVM classifiers, each optimized using a grid search for the best performance. Our final submission was an ensemble of these models, which performed offline evaluation within the top third of the competition. Notably, our models also demonstrated a moderate level of agreement with the provided human annotations. Additionally, we analyzed the characteristics of the UM-IU@LING dataset and our models to gain a deeper understanding of the task. Our study also highlights the limitations of relying on pre-trained language models and the importance of feature engineering in offensiveness classification. Ultimately, we successfully completed the competition and are pleased with our results. Our code is publicly available on GitHub for reproducibility purposes. Furthermore, we have uploaded our model's predictions to Figshare for the convenience of other researchers. Our team's website includes more detailed information about our work. A new computational framework is developed to simultaneously reconstruct multiple energy levels, reduce noise, and separate materials in CT images. Formulated as a non-convex variational problem, the approach incorporates prior information about the low-pass filter and the physical properties of the projection data. The system is cast as a total variation regularization term with data-driven weights that are data-dependent and anisotropic. The challenge of non-convexity is overcome by converting the problem into a convex optimization issue using surrogate functions. The proposed method is evaluated with simulated data across three applications: dual-energy CT, high-resolution CT, and multi-energy CT. The results show that the reconstructed images produced by the new framework are comparable to those obtained with conventional iterative methods. The study also highlights the potential of the framework to further improve image quality. We introduce a new approach called sturdiness assurance, which guarantees a Bayesian network's performance under uncertain data and parameters within predetermined limits. Our method involves loosening the constraints of a probabilistic circuit representing the network's parameters, yielding a polytope that encompasses all possible network outcomes. We develop an integer programming method to determine the sturdiness polytope's boundaries, along with a approximation technique via convex optimization. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through numerical case studies in machine learning and counterfactual reasoning. Our code is available online at the specified URL. We have developed a method to create polarization entanglement between two photons using a quantum scissors technique. This technique enables us to truncate the polarization space of a three-level atomic ensemble, generating entangled photons with distinct polarization states. Our approach offers several advantages over traditional methods, primarily due to the high success rate of entanglement production and the ability to create various entangled states quickly. Additionally, we have established a connection between the quantum scissors technique and a quantum teleportation protocol that utilizes a three-level atomic ensemble to transfer an unknown polarization state. Furthermore, we have demonstrated that the quantum scissors technique can be utilized to prepare other complex quantum states, such as Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger and cluster states. This method provides a simple means to create prominent polarization entanglement, making it a valuable resource for various quantum information processing applications. Moreover, we have analyzed the effects of decoherence on the entanglement and found that the quantum scissors technique remains more robust against decoherence than other methods. Finally, we have outlined potential pathways to experimentally implement the quantum scissors technique using advanced optical systems. This method holds significant potential for creating prominent polarization entanglement, enabling the development of novel quantum information processing applications and serving as a valuable tool for testing the principles of quantum mechanics and quantum information processing.

We introduce a novel analytical approach to solve Nash equilibrium problems in various applications. This method distorts the resolvent operator to facilitate exact symbolic calculation of equilibrium conditions. Our operator's distortion formula can be calculated straightforwardly and does not necessitate the smooth function differentiability requirement. We demonstrate its utility by solving symbolic Nash equilibrium equations in optimization, quadratic feedback control, and smooth permeability estimation problems. Additionally, we provide a C implementation of the operator's distortion formula.

To address this issue, we present a novel transformer network that uses the Shifted Window Cross-Focus (SWCF) attention mechanism, which is capable of handling multi-scale spatiotemporal dependencies. The SWCF combines the strengths of the Multi-Head Attention and Multi-Head Cross-Attention mechanisms, and outperforms them significantly in experiments. Furthermore, we evaluate the effectiveness of our proposed model on two climate prediction tasks: climate downscaling and climate forecasting. The results show that the model achieves state-of-the-art performance on the Climate Forecasting dataset and comparable performance on the Climate Downscaling dataset. We provide a precise estimate for the initial eigenvalue of a nonlinear elliptic operator with a Robin boundary condition, giving a sharp lower bound under minimal assumptions and a sharp upper bound under more stringent conditions. This research extends previous findings in both nonlinear Robin problems and Schrödinger operators to include a proof of monotone subadditivity in the Szegö recurrence theorem. The main tool employed is our modified version of the free boundary theory's blow-up method. This theory involves constructing a specific free boundary problem associated with each eigenfunction or eigenvector, where the blow-up rate is dictated by the eigenvalue or eigenvector itself. Notably, our approach allows for the consideration of Dirichlet boundary conditions, effectively generalizing existing first eigenvalue estimates to all positive dimensions. This generalization was previously hindered by a technical issue known as the "bad sign" problem, which we resolve through the development of new techniques. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our upper bound can be refined into an asymptotic expansion under more restrictive conditions. Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs) are a crucial component in graph-level deep learning, but their underlying mathematical foundation is complex and poorly understood. This complexity hinders developers' ability to design GCNNs, leading to a lack of clear guidelines and excessive reliance on heuristic methods. To address this issue, we introduce a new approach based on matched filtering that provides in-depth insight into GCNNs, effectively transforming them into traditional convolutional neural networks. This insight enables us to identify the essential requirements for graph filters to be graph convolutions, ultimately leading to the development of novel graph convolutional layers with improved computational efficiency and broader applicability. Additionally, we demonstrate how this framework can be utilized to design GCNNs for arbitrary graph representations and showcase its effectiveness in multiple graph classification benchmarks. The source code for this work is publicly available at https://github.com/zhaozhenggg/IGCN. The corresponding mathematical description can be found at https://zhaozhenggg.github.io/publication/ICN.

This paper introduces a contextualized self-learning approach for low-resource dependency parsing. It utilizes a pre-trained language model to generate contextualized dependencies, which are then enhanced with additional contextual information and used to construct a dependency parser through self-learning. We contextualized existing dependency parsing models and applied them to five low-resource languages. The experimental results demonstrate that our method yields significant improvements over the standard model and existing unsupervised and semi-supervised baselines. Furthermore, we contextualized the Biaffine parser, which achieved state-of-the-art performance in several high-resource languages, and applied it to five low-resource languages. The method led to substantial improvements over the unsupervised UPOS tagger and the current unsupervised dependency parsers. We also achieved notable enhancements in dependency parsing accuracy with only a few hundred annotated sentences in the target language. The source code is available at https://github.com/zhuyaqi/CSL.

This study introduces a novel concept, the heart of a set-valued function, which serves as a central, compact, and convex structure for two-dimensional set-valued functions. The heart's definition is grounded in the heart of a set, which was previously established as an upper semicontinuous property. In contrast, the heart of a set-valued function possesses continuous properties. Building on this framework, we demonstrate the existence of the heart for two-dimensional set-valued functions with Lipschitz property. Furthermore, we develop effective numerical methods to calculate the heart of Lipschitz set-valued functions, which includes a direct approach and an indirect method utilizing the heart of a set-decomposition technique. The proposed algorithms are supported by a range of illustrative examples and numerical simulations. The heart of a set-valued function concept holds significant potential for applications in various fields, such as optimal control, where it may be employed to simplify complex set-inclusive constraints. Our findings demonstrate that a compile-time neural network specialization approach can substantially decrease run-time costs, yielding comparable or even better accuracy and latency performance compared to existing run-time methods. Our study also highlights the significance of initial search space scope and inheritance in compile-time specialization. These outcomes provide valuable insights for the development of more efficient neural network configuration search techniques. A comprehensive open-source prototype is available online for replicating our research. This model incorporates a passive particle that acts as a "memory cell" to introduce persistence into the active particle's motion. Our research focuses on the Active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Particle model's active parameter, which we refer to as "labor." By adjusting the labor, we observe a wide range of active behaviors, from localized to global patterns. These patterns are stable in certain parameter regimes but become unstable in others. This finding is supported by numerical simulations, which demonstrate the active particle's behavior in different Labor regimes. This paper introduces HUMBI, a comprehensive dataset of human body gestures, captured through multiple viewpoints. The dataset was captured using high-resolution stereoscopic video and depth sensors, along with corresponding annotated sequences, spanning 40 hours of content. The HUMBI dataset is designed to facilitate the development of gesture recognition systems, encompassing view selection and alignment, reconstruction, and similarity analysis. The paper also outlines a benchmarking competition in conjunction with ECCV 2022, utilizing the HUMBI dataset to address these challenges. The competition's results reveal the effectiveness of state-of-the-art methods in utilizing diverse viewpoints and reconstructing gestures from various perspectives. The HUMBI dataset and competition code are publicly available at https://humbi.is.tu-clausthal.de/.

To facilitate cross-lingual transfer in NLP, we introduce Neural Task Depictions - a model-agnostic approach that provides weak supervision. NTDs depict NLP tasks as a task-specific word embedding space, which can be learned across languages. We utilize these representations to enhance model generalizability in zero-shot settings, achieving notable improvements in NLP tasks like sentiment analysis and question answering, outperforming existing methods and reaching 74.6% F1 in sentiment analysis with no task data and no target vocabulary. Our code is publicly available on GitHub.

A key task in video super-resolution is improving low-resolution video input to high-quality and smooth resolution using limited frames. Our approach, BasicVSR++, builds upon the previous method BasicVSR by enhancing video super-resolution with additional details and accurate frame alignment. The novel encoder design in BasicVSR++ captures more context and features with higher resolution, while FrameFormer++ replaces the BasicVSR encoder with improved performance. Furthermore, PFEA replaces the traditional spatial-temporal alignment technique with a more precise correlation metric. Our experiments show that BasicVSR++ significantly outperforms the competition on various benchmarks in PSNR, SSIM, and FVD. The code and models are available on https://github.com/haofuAI/BasicVSR++.

In real-world applications, reinforcement learning agents must process high-dimensional sensory data from multiple sources to accomplish a variety of tasks. However, current models are prone to failures when faced with several tasks that require sensory input. We present a novel training method that allows agents to perform a range of tasks while maintaining high performance, by decomposing the agent into separate modules that learn and generalize independently. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by showing significant improvements in robustness and performance compared to traditional training methods, particularly in challenging scenarios with sensory input. Our findings highlight the potential of modular systems to create resilient agents in complex environments.

We introduce a novel approach to image tone mapping that learns from a collection of images to produce a single output image with improved contrast. Our method employs two neural networks: one that analyzes a group of high-dynamic-range images to derive a global style, and another that uses that style to compress the dynamic range of a set of input images, selecting the most representative values. We also demonstrate a reverse process, style extraction, by training a network to recreate a high-dynamic-range image from a single low-dynamic-range image using the learned global style. Our experiments show that our method outperforms existing techniques in both forward and reverse tone mapping. We have made our code and data available for public use.

This study explores the behavior of a system driven by time-varying currents in random thermodynamics. We demonstrate the stationarity of a generalized fluctuation dissipativity theorem, yielding currents that are insensitive to time changes within their fluxes' calibration. We leverage this result to show the independence of asymptotic distributions of currents from flux calibrations, ultimately proving the stationarity of these distributions. This finding provides a solid foundation for the second part of this study.
